newsitem.title: ITALY: Zaire welcomes departure of Hutus refugees.
newsitem.headline: Zaire welcomes departure of Hutus refugees.

text.p: Zaire on Friday welcomed signs that hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees were returning to Rwanda and said it hoped that a mass exodus was finally under way.

But Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda hit out at international attitudes to the crisis and said Zaire reserved the right to veto participation by certain nations in a planned multinational relief force for the east of the country.

U.N. refugee officials in the town of Goma said on Friday at least 250,000 refugees, who had been trapped by fighting in eastern Zaire, were on the move and the entire population of refugee camps could be heading back to Rwanda.
The refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates with soldiers and militiamen who led the slaughter.
"I hope so with all my heart," Mutumbo told reporters at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome when asked whether the reverse flow was the start of a full-scale departure.
"I can't be moved that the refugees are going home -- whatever could be more natural," he said.
Mutombo said speakers at the summit had focused on the refugee crisis without concern for the suffering caused to Zaire's own people.
"The international community is mobilising in favour of the refugees and forgetting the Zaireans," he said.

"I followed the speeches of the high moral authorities who direct world organisations. I followed attentively. Nowhere in these speeches did they pay homage to my country. That is what's revolting. The victim becomes the accused," he said.
Mutombo on Thursday called for aid for refugees to be sent to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage them to return there.
Asked whether Zaire would block aid on its soil, he said: "Zaire is a sovereign country. Within its borders, Zaire can decide in a sovereign fashion."

The U.N. Security Council was expected on Friday to authorise the deployment of a multinational intervention force to help get food, water and medicine to the 1.2 million refugees stranded by fighting in the region and at urgent risk.
Mutombo said Zaire reserved the right to veto countries he said had been "accomplices of Rwanda in the aggression", supplying arms and military expertise. He refused to name names.
"Our government is waiting to be notified of the decision of the Security Council," he said. "We will see when we get the list which countries we can accept and which we cannot accept."
Diplomatic sources said the initial force, to be led by Canada, was expected to include troops from the United States, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.
Mutombo said the international community had "disappeared into thin air" after bringing initial relief in 1994, leaving Zaire to sort things out.

"If the international community comes back with aid, that will last as long as such and such an official in such and such a government needs to show his public opinion that he can bring aid, he'll get elected and then it will be finished," he said.
